summary:
Same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence in Côte d'Ivoire. The US State Department's 2023 country report on human rights practices records that same-sex relations are not an offence, so a trans visitor carries no statutory exposure on that ground.

Violence against LGBTQ people by non-state actors is documented and has been lethal. The 2023 report counts three deaths within the community during that year. Police handling of such violence was described as sometimes slow and ineffective and often inclined to blame the victim, although authorities were dealing with complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

Trans and gender-nonconforming people face the sharper risk. A transgender man was beaten in Abobo, a district of Abidjan, while walking with another man.

Peer-reviewed research published in 2015 found that travestis, people born male who live as women, endure harsher stigmatisation and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention. The same study reports that Ivoirian rights groups distanced themselves from travestis and underserved them, and it examines the isolation travestis experienced after the 2010-11 post-election violence.

Protection machinery is assessed from outside rather than through trans-specific statute. A United Nations development report of December 2024, reviewing ten years of a regional commission resolution on LGBT+ rights, includes a Côte d'Ivoire overview examining the protective legal environment, investigation and prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space and inclusion of LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The documented harm comes from private actors rather than from criminal law, so a visitor's exposure turns on public visibility and on how police respond to a complaint, not on the existence of a statute.

The 2011 US State Department human rights report on Côte d'Ivoire carries limited LGBT-specific content. It instead records the post-electoral crisis, with roughly 3,000 deaths, sexual violence and mass displacement, and that is the same period in which the 2015 study documents heightened isolation among travestis.

The December 2024 United Nations development report situates Côte d'Ivoire within a continental review of a regional human-rights commission resolution, so its assessment of the country's legal and civic environment is comparative rather than trans-specific.
localsOnly:
Ivoirian rights organisations have distanced themselves from travestis and left them underserved, according to the 2015 study, which limits the domestic support available to visibly gender-nonconforming residents.

The same study documents isolation among travestis following the 2010-11 post-election violence, a period when community networks were disrupted.

Domestic complaint-handling by authorities was reported as somewhat better than in previous years, even as police responses to violence committed by non-state actors remained slow, ineffective and prone to blaming the victim.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry, visa and identity-document screening rules specific to transgender travellers are not covered by any source in this inventory; that layer of the record remains unresolved rather than absent.

Where trans detainees are held, whether placement follows birth sex or gender identity, whether dedicated units exist, and whether solitary confinement or segregation is used are not covered in any listed Human Rights Watch publication. On the organisation's Côte d'Ivoire country page, LGBT Rights appears only as a topic-facet link.

A New York Times article dated October 2024 addresses LGBTQ conditions in Côte d'Ivoire, but the inventory specifies none of its findings, so no claim rests on it.

The United Nations development report's Côte d'Ivoire overview is known here only by the dimensions it assesses; its country-level conclusions are not reproduced in the inventory and would need direct verification.
